title: Paper 1 Question 4: Extended Response
description: The 250–300 word extended response to Text C — mining the bullet points, writing in role, and meeting the conventions of letters, reports, journals, speeches, interviews and articles.

notes.heading: The Shape of Question 4
notes.body: Question 4 is the last task on Paper 1 and the only one where you produce a complete text type. You respond to Text C in about 250–300 words, in ONE of six assigned forms: letter, report, journal, speech, interview or article. The 20 marks split evenly: 10 reading marks (R1, R2, R3, R5 — understanding the text, developing its ideas and selecting for your purpose) and 10 writing marks (W1–W4 — expression, structure, range, and language suited to audience and purpose). Note that W5 accuracy is not separately assessed here, though errors still blur meaning. Because Question 4 comes last, it is the question most often rushed — protect about 30–35 minutes for it and never let the earlier questions eat that time.

notes.heading: Mine the Bullets
notes.body: The question tells you exactly what to write through its bullet points. Each bullet is required content, and the reading marks are largely distributed across them: a three-bullet task that answers only two bullets has surrendered roughly a third of the content credit before style is even considered. Work methodically. Turn each bullet into a paragraph (or two), and find the lines in Text C that feed it — underline them before you draft, then tick each bullet off as you write it. The bullets also set the angle: 'explain why you disagreed with the decision' means every point must be filtered through disagreement, not merely listed. Treat the bullets as a checklist printed on the exam paper for your benefit — because that is exactly what they are.

illustration.alt: A four-step flow for Question 4: the task bullets lead to evidence mined from Text C, then to developed points in your assigned role, and finally into the frame of the assigned text type, with a bar showing the even split of 10 reading and 10 writing marks.
illustration.caption: Build a Question 4 answer in four steps: bullets, evidence, development, form. The 20 marks split evenly between reading and writing.

notes.heading: Adopt the Role — and Stay in Character
notes.body: Most Question 4 tasks assign you a role: a witness, a participant, a relative, a local resident. From the first sentence you ARE that person. Write with their knowledge (they cannot know facts from outside their world), their feelings (a survivor is not neutral), and their stake in events (a resident whose street will be demolished cares differently from a journalist passing through). Keep the voice consistent to the final line — slipping back into your own school-student voice, or summarising the text like an essay, breaks the spell and costs W4 marks for audience and purpose. Before writing, jot three words describing your role's emotional state and use them to colour every paragraph.

notes.heading: Develop and Evaluate — Do Not Just Repeat
notes.body: The reading marks include R3: analyse, evaluate and DEVELOP the text's ideas. A response that merely restates what Text C said, even in elegant prose, sits in the middle bands. Development means taking an idea further: what follows from it? What would your role add from their own experience? What example proves it — or complicates it? Evaluation means judging: is the writer's claim convincing, fair, complete? Where does it clash with what your role saw? A strong pattern for each bullet is: point from the text, then your role's extension or judgement of it. 'The report praised the new crossing — but I still watch children dodge the traffic every morning, so one crossing is a start, not a solution.'

notes.heading: Conventions: Letter, Report, Journal
notes.body: Markers reward text-type awareness (W4), so signal the assigned form from line one. Letter: your address and the date at the top, a salutation matched to the relationship ('Dear Ms Okafor' or 'Dear Grandma'), clear paragraphs, and a matching sign-off — 'Yours sincerely' after a named person, 'Yours faithfully' after 'Dear Sir/Madam', something warm for family. Report: a title, a brief statement of purpose, headed sections, and a formal, impersonal tone, often ending in recommendations. Journal (diary): the date, first person throughout, and an informal, reflective voice — feelings, doubts and hindsight are the whole point of the form. In every case the layout earns little on its own; it must wrap the required content from Text C.

notes.heading: Conventions: Speech, Interview, Article
notes.body: Speech: greet the audience directly ('Thank you for coming'), keep addressing them ('you', 'we'), use the spoken devices covered in Persuasive and Argumentative Writing — rhetorical questions, tricolons, direct appeals — and close with thanks or a call to action. Interview: present real turns, labelled or clearly framed ('Interviewer: ... Meera: ...'), with questions that probe the events of Text C and answers that stay in the interviewee's character. Article: a headline, an opening paragraph that hooks and orients the reader, and a sense of a public audience — livelier than a report, more organised than a journal. Whichever form you are assigned, the content still comes from Text C via the bullets; the form is the packaging, not the product.

notes.heading: Balancing the 10 + 10 Split
notes.body: Half the marks are reading and half are writing, so two failure modes mirror each other: the beautiful answer that ignores the bullets caps near 10 of 20, and the content-stuffed answer in the wrong voice does the same. Plan for both halves in about five minutes: tick the bullets, fix your persona's voice, and order the paragraphs. Aim for 250–300 words — under 200 almost always means under-developed content, and far over 300 usually means drifting off the bullets. Finish with a two-minute check: every bullet ticked? voice consistent? the form's conventions visible? To build fluency inside these constraints, write full timed answers against the course's free-response practice sets and review the AI marking feedback objective by objective.

flashcards.definition: Paper 1 Question 4: about 250–300 words on Text C in an assigned text type; 10 reading and 10 writing marks.
flashcards.example: A speech by the mountain guide from Text C, answering the task's bullets.

flashcards.definition: The bullet points printed in the question; each is required content and maps to the reading marks.
flashcards.example: Three bullets, two answered — roughly a third of the content credit gone.

flashcards.definition: The persona the task assigns you; you write as them — their knowledge, feelings and stake — throughout.
flashcards.example: Writing as the rescue volunteer, you cannot quote the mayor's private letter.

flashcards.definition: The level of formality and tone chosen to suit the audience and purpose (W4).
flashcards.example: A council report is formal; a journal entry is not.

flashcards.definition: Extending a point from the text with your role's reasoning, examples or consequences (R3).
flashcards.example: 'One crossing helps — but the school run needs a patrol too.'

flashcards.definition: Judging the text's ideas — how convincing, fair or complete they are — with support (R3).
flashcards.example: 'The claim rests on one survey of forty people.'

flashcards.definition: The greeting that opens a letter, matched to the reader.
flashcards.example: 'Dear Ms Okafor' to a named official; 'Dear Sir/Madam' when unknown.

flashcards.definition: A letter's closing, matched to its salutation.
flashcards.example: 'Yours sincerely' after a name; 'Yours faithfully' after 'Dear Sir/Madam'.

flashcards.definition: Date, first person, informal reflective voice; feelings and hindsight are the point of the form.
flashcards.example: 'Tuesday. I cannot stop replaying the moment the rope went slack.'

flashcards.definition: Title, statement of purpose, headed sections, formal impersonal tone, often recommendations.
flashcards.example: 'To: The School Council. Purpose: to review the canteen queue.'

flashcards.definition: Labelled or clearly framed question-and-answer exchanges between interviewer and interviewee.
flashcards.example: 'Interviewer: Were you afraid? Meera: Terrified — and I'd do it again.'

flashcards.definition: An article's title; pair it with an opening paragraph that hooks the reader and sets the angle.
flashcards.example: 'Our Street, Their Bulldozers: The Fight Starts Here'

questions.stem: About how many words should a Question 4 response be?
choices: No more than 120 words
About 250–300 words
About 350–450 words
550–650 words
questions.explanation: Question 4 specifies about 250–300 words. The 120-word ceiling is the 2(a) summary; 350–450 is the Paper 2 Section B composition; and 550–650 is the length of the Paper 2 Section A reading texts — nothing you write.

questions.stem: Which set lists only text types that Question 4 can assign?
choices: Essay, short story, poem or play script
Summary, comprehension answers or language analysis
Letter, report, journal, speech, interview or article
Any form you prefer — the choice is yours
questions.explanation: The syllabus fixes six forms for Q4 — letter, report, journal, speech, interview and article — and the question assigns ONE of them. Narrative and descriptive composition belong to Paper 2 Section B; summaries and analysis are Questions 2 and 3; and you never choose the form yourself.

questions.stem: A Q4 task asks for a letter from the mayor to residents with three bullets: explain why the scheme was approved; respond to concerns about noise; describe what happens next. A student covers the first bullet brilliantly but never mentions noise or next steps. What is the likely cost?
choices: Potentially around two-thirds of the reading marks — the bullets are required content, however brilliant the rest is
Nothing — writing quality fully compensates
Only writing marks, since the letter's content is complete
A fixed penalty of exactly five marks
questions.explanation: The bullets distribute the 10 reading marks; ignoring two of three forfeits most of that credit no matter how strong the surviving paragraph is. Writing marks cannot buy back reading credit, the content is by definition incomplete, and marking is best-fit, not a fixed-penalty table.

questions.stem: In a Question 4 letter, the salutation is:
choices: the final paragraph
the headline
the writer's own address
the greeting that opens the letter, such as 'Dear Ms Okafor'
questions.explanation: The salutation is the opening greeting, chosen to fit the relationship. The closing paragraph and the writer's address sit elsewhere in the layout, and letters do not have headlines — that is the article convention.

questions.stem: You must write a journal entry as the rescue volunteer from Text C. Which sentence best fits the role and the form?
choices: 'The rescue operation was conducted efficiently by trained volunteers.'
'Volunteers often report mixed feelings after a rescue.'
'My hands are still shaking as I write this — but I would wade in again tomorrow.'
'This entry will analyse the rescue from several perspectives.'
questions.explanation: The third option is first-person, emotional and immediate — a journal in the volunteer's own voice. The first reads like an official report (impersonal passive), the second is a detached generalisation about volunteers, and the last announces an essay, which neither the form nor the role allows.

questions.stem: Text C argues that a new cycle lane has reduced accidents. Which sentence DEVELOPS this idea rather than repeating it?
choices: 'If accidents have fallen, the same logic justifies extending the lane past the school, where the risk is greatest.'
'The cycle lane has reduced accidents.'
'The writer says the cycle lane has reduced accidents.'
'I completely agree with the writer about the cycle lane.'
questions.explanation: The first option extends the text's claim to a new situation with a reason — that is R3 development. The middle two merely restate or report the claim, and empty agreement without reasoning earns nothing either.

questions.stem: A student's Q4 speech covers every bullet accurately, but addresses the audience only once — a 'thank you' in the final line. What is the main weakness?
choices: Nothing — content coverage is all Question 4 tests
The speech is automatically too short to score
The student has broken the word limit
Half the marks are writing marks, and W4 rewards sustained audience engagement — one 'thank you' is not a speech register
questions.explanation: A speech must sound spoken: direct address, inclusive 'we', rhetorical devices throughout. Content coverage is only the reading half of the marks; nothing here indicates a length problem; and a single closing pleasantry cannot carry W4 on its own.

questions.stem: Which text type is dated, written in the first person, and reflective?
choices: Report
Journal
Article
Interview
questions.explanation: The journal (diary) is defined by date, first person and reflection on feelings. A report is formal and impersonal, an article addresses the public, and an interview is a two-voice exchange.

questions.stem: A Question 4 report to the school council should open with:
choices: 'Dear Council, how are you?'
'Once upon a time'
a title and a brief statement of the report's purpose, followed by headed sections
a rhetorical question and a joke to warm the reader up
questions.explanation: Reports are formal and impersonal: title, purpose, headed sections. A friendly letter opening confuses the form; a story opening belongs to narrative; and jokes suit some speeches or articles, not a report to the council.

questions.stem: Which sentence best shows EVALUATION of Text C's claim that homework should be abolished?
choices: 'The writer thinks homework should be abolished.'
'The claim rests on one school's survey; until harder evidence exists, abolition is a gamble rather than a policy.'
'Homework is a controversial topic with many possible opinions.'
'I totally agree — homework is pointless.'
questions.explanation: Evaluation weighs the quality of the idea: the second option probes the evidence base and judges the risk, with reasoning. The first only reports the claim, the third gestures at controversy without judging anything, and the last is an unsupported opinion — assertion is not evaluation.

questions.stem: How are the 20 marks for Question 4 divided?
choices: 10 for reading and 10 for writing
15 for reading and 5 for writing
All 20 for writing
All 20 for reading
questions.explanation: Question 4 splits evenly: 10 reading marks (R1, R2, R3, R5) and 10 writing marks (W1–W4). An all-reading split would make your text-type craft worthless; an all-writing split would make Text C irrelevant — the task deliberately tests both at once.

questions.stem: Which layout best presents a Question 4 interview?
choices: A continuous-prose retelling of what was said
A long speech by the interviewee alone
A letter containing the interviewee's answers
Labelled turns — 'Interviewer:' and 'Priya:' — with questions that probe the events of Text C
questions.explanation: An interview is an exchange: framed turns, probing questions, answers in character. Prose summary erases the questioner; a monologue is a speech, not an interview; and a letter is a different assigned form with its own conventions.

questions.stem: A student answers every bullet but finishes in 160 words. What is the best advice?
choices: Submit it — there is no minimum length to worry about
Develop each bullet further; 160 words in a 250–300 word task suggests under-developed ideas
Pad the ending with a long quotation from Text C
Add a second text type to fill the space
questions.explanation: The 250–300 word guidance is a signal about depth: covering the bullets thinly leaves R3 development marks on the table. Quotation padding is lifting in disguise, and bolting on a second form breaks the assigned text type.

questions.stem: A student says: 'Question 4 is really a comprehension test — get the content down and the style takes care of itself.' Why is this wrong?
choices: It is not wrong — content decides everything
Style is only assessed in Paper 2, never Paper 1
Half the marks (W1–W4) reward expression, organisation, range and audience awareness, so content alone caps the score near 10 of 20
The bullet points test writing, not reading
questions.explanation: The 10 + 10 split means a content-perfect but flat answer strands half the marks. Style is very much assessed on Paper 1; and the bullets feed the reading marks, with the writing marks rewarding how you deliver that content in the assigned form and voice.

questions.stem: When do you decide which of the six text types to write in Question 4?
choices: Immediately — the question assigns one specific form, and you must write that one
After the first paragraph, once you see how it feels
Whichever you like — all six are always on offer
Only if time remains at the end
questions.explanation: The task specifies one of the six forms, and using it is part of the brief (W4). Choosing your favourite, drifting between forms, or treating the form as optional all ignore an instruction the marker is checking for.
